original_claim_summary: The entry combines an approximately $880 billion Medicaid cut with more than 8 million uninsured people and applies those numbers to a single bill version without clarifying its date.

source_urls.access_notes: CBO June 24, 2025 estimate reviewed; it concerns H.R. 1 as passed by the House on May 22, 2025.
supports: CBO estimated that the House-passed Medicaid provisions would increase the uninsured population by 7.8 million in 2034 relative to current-law baseline projections.

source_urls.access_notes: KFF analysis identifies the House-passed bill and its estimate vintage.
supports: KFF reports the House-passed bill's Medicaid provisions would reduce federal Medicaid spending by $793 billion and increase uninsured by 7.8 million in 2034; it distinguishes a separate 10.3-million Medicaid enrollment decline.

supported_facts: For the House-passed H.R. 1, CBO's estimate was 7.8 million more uninsured people in 2034 from Medicaid provisions.
KFF reports a $793 billion federal Medicaid spending reduction for that House-passed version and distinguishes the separate enrollment estimate from the uninsured count.
unsupported_original_claims: The entry combines an approximately $880 billion cut associated with a later bill version with the House-passed 8-million-plus uninsured estimate.
'Lose healthcare' is imprecise: the CBO measure is a projected increase in people without insurance in 2034, relative to baseline, not a count of identifiable people already losing coverage.
Claims about disproportionate effects, preventable deaths, or state-specific responses are not established by these two sources.

narrow_corrected_claim.title: House-passed H.R. 1 Medicaid provisions projected to add 7.8 million uninsured
narrow_corrected_claim.claim: CBO estimated that Medicaid provisions in H.R. 1 as passed by the House on May 22, 2025 would increase the number of uninsured people by 7.8 million in 2034 relative to current law. KFF reports a $793 billion federal Medicaid spending reduction for that version; later bill versions received separate estimates.

exact_evidence_gap: The original does not identify the bill version or baseline, and the $880 billion figure does not belong with the House-passed estimate documented here; no evidence in these sources supports the claimed preventable-death outcome.
disposition_rationale: Use the House-passed version's matched estimate and distinguish uninsured people from Medicaid enrollment losses and spending reductions.

original_claim_summary: Trump allegedly signed an executive order in April 2017 that cut Medicaid work requirements and caused states to impose work rules.

supports: CMS announced that states could seek Section 1115 demonstration waivers to test community-engagement requirements for certain Medicaid beneficiaries.
The policy was agency guidance for state waiver proposals, not an executive order establishing a national work requirement.

source_urls.access_notes: CMS overview of state Section 1115 demonstration waiver authority.
supports: Section 1115 demonstrations require federal approval and are state-specific.

supported_facts: On January 11, 2018, CMS issued guidance permitting states to request Section 1115 waivers for community-engagement demonstrations.
States needed federal approval for individual waiver proposals; the guidance did not itself create a nationwide mandate.
unsupported_original_claims: No cited source supports a Trump executive order in April 2017 establishing Medicaid work requirements.
The CMS action was 2018 agency guidance rather than a signed executive order.

The source does not establish that Arkansas was first to implement, that 18,000 people lost coverage within a year, or that courts later struck down 'many' waivers; those are separate claims requiring their own records.

narrow_corrected_claim.title: CMS guidance lets states seek Medicaid community-engagement waivers
narrow_corrected_claim.claim: On January 11, 2018, CMS said states could seek Section 1115 waivers to test community-engagement requirements for some Medicaid beneficiaries. The guidance enabled state-specific demonstrations subject to federal approval; it was not a 2017 executive order or a nationwide rule.

exact_evidence_gap: The source documents the waiver pathway only; it does not establish the later results, enrollment losses, court rulings, or an executive action in April 2017.
disposition_rationale: Correct the date and mechanism, and leave state implementation outcomes to separately sourced entries.

original_claim_summary: The Trump administration allegedly ended ACA enhanced premium subsidies in March 2025, shortened enrollment, and cut Navigator funding by 90%.

supports: CMS announced $10 million in federal Navigator program grants for the next plan year, a reduction from the prior $100 million level.

source_urls.access_notes: KFF FAQ updated January 14, 2026; reviewed for the actual tax-credit expiration date.
supports: The enhanced premium tax credit provisions expired at the end of 2025 and had not been renewed as of the FAQ update.
Navigator funding fell from $100 million for plan year 2025 to $10 million for plan year 2026, a 90% reduction.

supported_facts: CMS announced a reduction in Navigator funding to $10 million in February 2025, down from $100 million for the previous plan year.
Enhanced ACA premium tax credits continued through the end of 2025 and expired at year-end absent congressional extension; the expiry was not a March 2025 action.
The two facts concern separate actions and timelines.
unsupported_original_claims: The enhanced subsidies were not ended in March 2025; they expired after December 31, 2025.
The sources here do not establish that the administration shortened the enrollment period in March 2025.
The Navigator cut does not itself prove that millions lost coverage or that the combined actions constituted a backdoor repeal.

narrow_corrected_claim.title: CMS cuts ACA Navigator funding to $10 million; enhanced credits expire at 2025 year-end
narrow_corrected_claim.claim: CMS announced in February 2025 that Navigator grants would fall from $100 million to $10 million for the next plan year. Enhanced Marketplace premium tax credits remained in effect through December 31, 2025 and then expired absent extension. These are separate policy events, not a March subsidy termination.

exact_evidence_gap: No source reviewed supports a March 2025 end to enhanced subsidies or the stated enrollment-window change; the Navigator funding action is sourced separately.
disposition_rationale: Correct the timing and distinguish the documented Navigator reduction from the later statutory subsidy expiration.

original_claim_summary: Trump allegedly signed an executive order banning transgender students from girls' sports at federally funded schools on January 20, 2025.

supports: The order directs federal agencies to interpret and enforce Title IX against schools permitting transgender girls and women to compete in female sports categories, and directs action concerning federal funding.

supported_facts: Trump signed the sports executive order on February 5, 2025, not January 20.
The order directed federal agencies to use the administration's stated Title IX interpretation and to review federal funding consequences for covered schools.
unsupported_original_claims: The executive order's signing does not itself establish that every federally funded school immediately implemented a blanket ban or lost funding.
The cited order does not substantiate a documented post-order surge in bullying or medical-outcome claims.

narrow_corrected_claim.title: Trump signs Title IX sports executive order on February 5, 2025
narrow_corrected_claim.claim: On February 5, 2025, Trump signed an executive order directing agencies to enforce the administration's interpretation of Title IX against schools that allow transgender girls and women to compete in female sports categories, including review of federal-funding consequences. The order's issuance does not establish immediate implementation at every school.

exact_evidence_gap: The cited order supports the directive and date but does not establish the realized effect on each federally funded school, any specific funding termination, or the reported student-health outcomes.
disposition_rationale: Correct the signing date and describe the executive directive without presenting its intended enforcement as a completed nationwide outcome.

original_claim_summary: In February 2025, Trump allegedly issued an executive order and proposed legislation stripping federal courts of authority to issue nationwide injunctions.

source_urls.source_type: news reporting on Supreme Court litigation
source_urls.access_notes: Reuters article text reviewed; describes the administration's March 2025 Supreme Court filing in birthright-citizenship litigation.
supports: In March 2025, the administration asked the Supreme Court to limit the scope of nationwide injunctions blocking Trump's birthright-citizenship order.
The dispute concerned the remedy available in that litigation, rather than an enacted law stripping district courts of jurisdiction.

supported_facts: The administration sought Supreme Court review in March 2025 and argued for narrower relief in litigation over the birthright-citizenship order.
This was a litigation position about nationwide injunctions, not a completed change to courts' authority.
unsupported_original_claims: No source reviewed establishes the asserted February executive order or legislative proposal described in the entry.
The Reuters report does not say the administration had stripped courts of authority or that courts had lost power to grant broader relief.

narrow_corrected_claim.title: Trump administration asks Supreme Court to narrow birthright-citizenship injunctions
narrow_corrected_claim.claim: In March 2025, the Trump administration asked the Supreme Court to limit nationwide injunctions blocking its birthright-citizenship order. The request was a litigation argument about available relief, not an executive order removing federal courts' authority.

exact_evidence_gap: The evidence supports a March court filing but not the entry's February executive-order/legislative mechanism or any completed removal of judicial authority.
disposition_rationale: Replace the unsupported policy mechanism with the documented Supreme Court request and describe it as advocacy in pending litigation.
